newsitem.title: GHANA: World Bank head tells Ghana to cut public spending.
newsitem.headline: World Bank head tells Ghana to cut public spending.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn told Ghana on Wednesday to cut public spending, saying that it was stifling the development of the private sector in the West African nation.
At the same time, Wolfensohn, wrapping up the second leg of a nine-day African tour, said that tight economic management was the key to attracting private foreign investment.

"Rigorous economic management is an essential precondition to the creation of a proper environment for growth," he told a news conference before leaving for South Africa, adding that this would boost inflows of investment.
Throughout his visit, which began in Senegal at the weekend, Wolfensohn has stressed the need to open up African economies to the private sector, saying that Africa is the Bank's top priority.
He has also denounced corruption, saying the Bank will maintain a black list of guilty individuals and refuse to deal with them.
The World Bank once hailed Ghana as a model pupil and an example to other Africann countries in its economic adjustment.

Wolfensohn acknowledged that since 1992, when President Jerry Rawlings and his government made the mistake of hiking civil servants' pay by 80 percent before elections, Ghana had found the going tough.
"It is clear that in the last couple of years the growth is less than Ghanaians want," he said, adding that he believed that the government fully recognised the need for economic rigour.
"What they have in mind is to try, first of all, to contain inflation, which has an effect on the money supply and one of the ways of doing that is to not overspend," he said.
"This is not just a Ghanaian problem, this is a universal problem," he added.

He said that government overspending stifled the investment environment by forcing an increase in the money supply and fueling inflation. "If you have overspending on the part of government and therefore overborrowing on the part of government, the private sector is squeezed out."
Wolfensohn, who ends his tour in Mozambique, held talks with Rawlings on Wednesday.
The talks focused on efforts to boost farm production -- which occupies most of Ghana's 18 million people -- as part of a programme of integrated rural development.

This will seek to combine new production projects with quality of life projects. "Poverty in rural areas, the lack of clean water, the lack of educational access, particularly for young girls, is the sort of thing which will come under review, and which I think rural investment will make a difference to," Wolfensohn said.
On the liberalisation of cocoa exports, which are a major source of foreign exchange and which are still a state monopoly in Ghana, he said:
"We are very much in favour of free markets but it is for the government to decide how it wants to do it."
